title: Ideation: Dustwalker, an exploration journey through life after humans. Slop or not?
author: Lumpy_Conference6640
selftext:
**Dustwalker** is an early concept for a quiet exploration game set long after humans are gone. You play a small, caped robot crossing a desert of half-buried skyscrapers, following glowing glyphs toward a dead satellite on the horizon. Think *Journey* meets *Shadow of the Colossus*, with almost no UI. The only HUD is the energy trail streaming off the robot’s cape.

**What you’re seeing:** an animated gameplay mockup, not a playable build. There’s no code behind it yet. I’m using AI to explore the look and feel before committing to anything.

**Workflow**

1. Brainstormed the concept and wrote the image prompts with Claude: title screen plus gameplay screen, with a shared palette (warm sand, burnt orange, dusty rose) so they read as one game.
2. Generated the stills in \[tool name\] and picked the best of four.
3. Animated the gameplay still with image-to-video Veo: slow tracking camera, cape and sand motion, glowing glyph pulse.

**Why I’m asking “slop or not?”:** I’m trying to figure out whether this is useful as a pitch and art-direction reference, or whether it’s just pretty pictures with no game under them. My take is that it’s ideation, and the real test is whether I can build the actual game loop (traversal, glyph puzzles, environmental storytelling) in a way that lives up to the mockup.

**Questions for you:**

* Does this read as a coherent game concept, or as generic AI desert aesthetic?
* What would make it feel less like slop: a prototype, a mechanic demo, hand-made assets?
* Anyone gone from AI concept art to a real playable? What was your pipeline?

Happy to share the prompts if people want them.

comments.author: Beginning-Search-983
comments.body:
As a player, I think I'd want strong game play and a story and ending worth the journey. If it's just walking around and discovering lore through background details or found records or something, then, not for me (though some people love that stuff). It would at least need puzzles... something to actually do.

Basically I think it needs a mystery that you can actually participate in solving, instead of having it given to you by finding different texts or something. Or if you want more action, then the action parts need to feel like they're part of the world/universe. Because the game is about being in a post-human world, so the world and its story is important.

replies.author: sufficientgatsby
replies.body:
I think you'll need to refine the premise that you present with your game. "A robot explores the last vestiges of humanity" doesn't really invite much interest. A premise should include your inciting incident and the action/goal a character undertakes to address it. You need an event that causes your character to be in crisis and specific stakes.

For example- Did the robot's creator vanish or something? Why would that be urgent or catastrophic for the robot? What interesting actions must the robot now undertake to find its lost creator, and what major obstacles or antagonists are in its way?

It could be very problematic to have a main character "without purpose."

comments.author: DubiousTomato
comments.body:
As is, it really is just *Journey* but with a robot. It's not super compelling to me right now because it reads like a cheap reskin. I think if you're gonna do something like this, you need a hook that relates more to a theme about what you want to stick with the player. Right now, walking around in a desert doesn't tell me much about how the robot relates to the world, what it wants to achieve, or what you want to communicate about the world other than it being desolate. Where do you want the player to start, and where do you want the player to end, not purely location-wise, but emotionally?  
  
In terms of being executable I think creating a table of priorities would be important. Atmospheric games live and die on stylization, sound design, and story. I think this is fairly generic in both style and sound (I understand it's more a test than anything), although the idea of using a monochromatic color scheme could be a nice angle. I would be more deliberate about the color palette than this though. Leave space for imagination to fill in visual detail. The story isn't obvious yet, so I think there's room to play with the sense of intimacy between the character and the world they live in (the world feels a bit small here and it's hard to get a sense of scale overall due to the camera angle).

comments.author: TopTippityTop
comments.body:
1. The overall mood is well done. I like the vfx, lighting, models.
2. The robot concept doesn't seem strong. Hard to tell, really, as we don't get a good shot... But it just seems like a normal biped human with some stylized proportions. Not an interesting silhouette. Doesn't tell a story. Why a cape? Why.does it look the way it does? What was its function? It's visuals should match its prior function + the change in circumstances... It should tell a stroy about the character and ideally be recognizable from the silhouette.
3. Likewise, the environment should tell a story. It's about exploration. So ok, the area looks ruined, and that is the beginning of a story... But if you want to intrigue, then tell more. What happened? How did this specific area get ruined, and how is that reflected in the visuals?
4. Why are there glowing tendrils coming out of the character? It could work, but I'm not yet convinced from the video. The premise seems like a fairly realistic one... Humans get wrecked, a robot survived. The magical glowing tendrils detract from that tangibility and believability. So they need a pretty strong reason to be there imo.
5. Finally, the theme has been done in many ways. That's OK, but it won't be the thing which moves people at first. You need more imo. It's a good start, don't get me wrong, but I wouldn't treat it as the representative slice yet. What is relatable yet novel enough to get eyeballs? Need some more novel aspect. Random large thing fallen in the background has been overplayed. Not that it can't add, but it won't carry. This aspect doesn't have to be answered in this area, it could be something else about the world you introduce fairly early on that hooks... But since this is all you've give us, I'm adding the point to my feedback.

comments.author: Briskfall
comments.body:
The visuals looked sick I was about to say, then you dropped that it wasn't coded and I felt slightly betrayed. lol.

I have my own way of determining if it's slop or not but the core thing is, does this idea seem fun... to you?

Like even for handcrafted games, the concept of powerwash simulator seemed so ridiculous and sloplike but if it makes people *have fun*  \-- then I'd think that it's worthwhile.

Everyone has their own criteria of what is slop or not. There are some big AAA that I would call boring and padded despite scoring good reviews by early phase.

I guess the most important thing is to not be embarrassed about your idea, if you think that you struck gold. There are some people whose ideas I've seen to some... felt like absolute slop but to some others, it felt like an untapped market.

Personally, I would decide from a first impression by... the five minute mark. Make that first five minute *good*, look for play testers for the demo. And if it's all good, stretch it to fifteen, then thirty, and etc. Test your own game, and if the idea isn't speaking to you anymore -- maybe it's slop. You need to try to let the vision grow first.

As for the premise you've given to me so far... personally, it doesn't seem very interesting. I am not very confident in how a non sapien protagonist (reason is kinda long) for the early game would work. But that's just me.

comments.author: Lumpy_Conference6640

If you read some of the comments, I kinda learned a lot. Both about my game idea and design, and how players are making games. Also, one person said cart before the horse. I'm noticing people think that having AI means you should just start a project right away. 

In the past, we would storyboard and animate stills to plan the scope and ambience of games. From a project management aspect, you would build a requirements, roadmap, and establish your high poles for technical feasibility. 

Then you would engage with an audience, see their feedback one way or another, and decide how to modify your time and focus. 

Now everyone is like, just DO IT, and I get that with AI, barriers are reduced, but umm I still think if you're making a game for players, you might want to circle back to the fundamentals.

comments.author: AlexFaden
comments.body:
This screams heavily "inferior Journey clone" to me. And not really because of 100% obvious AI generated video. But because Journey was really soulful and visually stunning journey. with nearly the same features you are describing minus robots.(look it up) It is a beautiful piece of art that i doubt any AI can replicated it currently.

My honest take. Making a high fidelity game with entirely AI assets right now, not just using AI for prototyping, is waste of compute. Visual consistency for AI is still the biggest problem, together with that uncanny valley feel. Of course if you are a good at 3d modelling and animation yourself then go for it, but that would take a lot of time to do it all solo, unless you have enough money to buy up a bunch of assets.

Personally i am making a rouge like(lite) cyberpunk RPG on a primitive visual scale and high gameplay complexity of Dwarf Fortress and Cataclysm DDA. That is one of the few things you can program with AI really good without anyone able to tell that you used AI. Provided you can properly design all the systems yourself with AI just acting like a helper to point out things where you fucked up. But that is niche game genre and you have to do a lot of theory crafting on game mechanics and world simulation. I treat it mostly like a hobby product and will never expect to make much money from it.

comments.author: AsparagusOk8818
comments.body:
i mean... you have to play it first to know if the concept works. A purely visual 'mock-up' where you just tell an LLM to make an animation can't tell you anything beyond that the visuals could potentially be pretty, maybe, if you can get Tripo and/or Meshy to behave in the way you want. 

Prototype the experience first. If you want something like Journey, the emotional beats are everything. How are you going to deliver those? The premise has a lot of potential, but just wandering through ruins isn't going to create engagement. 

This is one of the hardest types of experiences to make - which isn't to say you shouldn't try, but it is to say that you should be prepared for an extraordinarily difficult task even though the premise is simple. You are asking the player to be vulnerable and throw away their irony armour for a while. That's a big ask. 

Develop the emotional core for the experience, and test it. You probably need to prototype that as part of an experience that isn't even video game-shaped. Once you have something that you think can be an effective and earnest delivery, connect with someone you trust and who you know will deliver honest feedback and give them that experience. See how they respond. 

  
The thing that makes these kinds of experiences special (and also the thing that makes some people always lash out about them) is that they're not just games - they're mirrors. Sometimes unflattering ones. 

Go watch the Carousel scene from Mad Men. That's what you're trying to do. 

It is a very formidable challenge.
